      7. The Lebesgue integral of non-negative functions#

      For a non-negative function on an interval of , the Riemann integral measures the area below its graph by summing the areas of thin vertical rectangles. On a general measure space , however, the domain need not possess a topological structure, an interval structure, or a linear order. Consequently, vertical partitioning is unavailable.

      The Lebesgue integral solves this problem by partitioning the subgraph into horizontal slices instead. At height , the horizontal slice corresponds to the set of points where , and its ``area’’ is measured using . In these notes, we construct the Lebesgue integral via these horizontal superlevel sets, establish its agreement with simple-function integrals, and prove its first approximation and linearity properties.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Define the non-negative Lebesgue integral from the measures of its superlevel sets.

      • Relate the superlevel-set definition to the finite-sum formula for a simple function.

      • Compute the integral of a simple function.

      • Define the Archimedean integral for non-increasing functions.

      • Prove the monotone convergence theorem for the Lebesgue integral and relate it to the monotone convergence properties of the Archimedean integral.

      • Deduce positive linearity from simple-function approximation and monotone convergence.

      Throughout these notes, denotes a measure space and all functions under consideration are measurable. Arithmetic for non-negative integrals takes place in , with the standard convention .

      7.2.3 Overlapping indicator representations#

      We have defined the integral and proved that it has the intuitive meaning we expect. However, we do not yet have one of its most important properties: linearity. We will first establish linearity for simple functions. To do so, we need to know that the values-times-measures sum depends only on the simple function, not on its particular indicator representation. The preceding proposition evaluates this sum for a pairwise-disjoint representation; we now extend it to representations whose indicator sets overlap.
